meaning.evidence: Every point survives: the deceptively simple task, compliance as the hard part, "hire a contractor or put extra strain on your agency", FedRAMP, previews and signoff, and all four static-site advantages, down to "where you only pay for what you use".

sense.evidence: Terms fit: "getting the security and privacy compliance sorted", "headaches like maintaining server applications", "It's dead easy to host", "a few things going for them".

authenticity.evidence: Natural Australian workplace English: "The hardest bit often isn't writing the content", "so you can put your know-how into your content", with Australian spelling "customisable", "organisation".

register.evidence: Lighter than level 3: mostly the original lightly reworded, with a handful of Aussie touches ("sorted", "bit", "dead easy", "headaches"); reads nearer level 2. No swearing, within the brief.

tone.evidence: Keeps the friendly, persuasive product-page tone: "It shouldn't be like that." and "you can count on your site being fast, reliable".

flow.evidence: Smooth throughout: "That way your team knows their changes will show up right when they're pushed to the main site".

variety.evidence: No slang leaned on, but "look after" recurs ("launch and look after", "easier to look after", "Pages looks after") and "steering clear" is doubled.

essence.evidence: Unmistakably the cloud.gov Pages pitch, same structure, headings and points: "Static websites have a few things going for them".

meaning.evidence: All points survive: "the hard yakka usually isn't writing the content or designing the site. It's getting the security and privacy compliance sorted", "bring in a contractor or load up your agency's web team even more", FedRAMP, previews, and the four advantages.

sense.evidence: Each term fits: "hard yakka" for the hardest part, "no drama" for easy signoff, "dead easy", "without any fuss", "a fair bit going for them".

register.evidence: Right at level 3: a steady, conversational Aussie layer ("chances are", "hard yakka", "no drama", "dead easy") on a page that still reads as a product page; no swearing, which suits it.

meaning.evidence: All points survive: "knock up a website as part of some initiative at your agency", compliance as the hard bit, "pile extra work on your agency's web team", FedRAMP, previews, and the four advantages through "show data from a separate server".

sense.evidence: Mostly exact ("compliance grunt work", "fewer weak spots", "dead easy"), but "get the tick-off on content updates" strains: a "tick-off" is a telling off, where "the tick" or "sign-off" is meant.

meaning.evidence: All the original's points are there, but colour adds claims: "and they're already flat out", "And they don't just wave anyone through.", and "odds are some bright spark's handed you a job" adds a sneer at whoever assigned it.

sense.evidence: Mostly apt ("hard yakka", "have a squiz before anything goes live", "box and dice", "schmick"), but "some bright spark" is sarcastic, casting the requester as foolish, and "some mongrel to poke at" stretches "vulnerabilities" into attackers.

register.evidence: Far heavier than level 3: a pub-talk product page with a quip on nearly every line ("The whole shebang.", "I reckon", "No paying for the whole box and dice"). The swearing ("the bloody security and privacy compliance", "some mongrel") stays within vulgarity 1.

tone.evidence: The persuasive pitch survives, but it turns sardonic and blokey for a government service page: "some bright spark's handed you", "It's getting the bloody security and privacy compliance sorted".

flow.evidence: Reads aloud with energy, but the tags pile up: "dozens of the things", "thank you very much", "The whole shebang."
